children: By Eliot Brown and Evan Gershkovich

U.S. relations with the Caucasus country of Georgia have gone from warm to frigid in recent years, as the former Soviet republic has cracked down on dissent and swung closer to Vladimir Putin's Russia.
One U.S. business undeterred by the shift: the Trump Organization.

This week, a set of Georgian developers are planning to launch marketing on the Trump Tower Tbilisi, unveiling renderings on a skyscraper poised to be the country's tallest. The Georgian investment firms signed a branding deal with the Trump family company in May for the 70-story tower.

It is a booming market for foreign Trump towers, as private developers from Abu Dhabi to Vietnam to the Maldives over the past three years have lined up to adorn their hotel and golf course projects with the Trump name.

During President Trump's first term, amid concerns over conflicts of interest, the Trump Organization vowed not to do any foreign deals, effectively bringing new business to a halt. But in Trump's second term, the president's business dropped that self-imposed limit-and deals are pouring in.
Last year, the president reported taking in $59 million from foreign property licensing deals, up from $45 million in 2024 and far more than any other year reported.

Developers typically pay the Trump Organization an upfront fee-recently around $5 million-then a portion of revenue, though specifics can vary. Much like a restaurant franchisee, developers in return can brand their projects as a Trump tower, so long as it conforms to various design and service standards. The Trump family often helps market the projects, appearing at public events.

Trump has said his sons run the business on his behalf and he isn't involved. The Trump Organization declined to comment. It has previously denied any conflict of interest, saying the business dealings are kept separate from administration policy.

Democrats and governance groups have said the income from around the globe introduces new potential conflicts to the president's foreign agenda. Some of the developers paying the Trump Organization have other business before the U.S. government.

The White House has said that Trump only acts in the best interests of the American public, and that there are no conflicts of interest with his businesses. A White House spokesperson didn't respond to a request for comment.
The prospect of Georgia's tallest tower rising with the Trump name strikes a note of particular foreign policy discord.

Georgia was once one of the U.S.'s closest partners among former Soviet states: George W. Bush flew to Tbilisi to declare it a "beacon of Liberty" in 2005, and the country was a candidate to join the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. The relationship has deteriorated since, as Georgia's ruling party-Georgian Dream-has drawn U.S. ire for legislation that cracks down on dissent and other moves that hewed closer to Russia.

The Biden administration publicly criticized the democratic backsliding, and relations have been chilly in the Trump administration: Secretary of State Marco Rubio appeared to refer to Georgia as having an "anti-American government" in a hearing last year.
Meanwhile, the project has given financial benefit to the family of a Georgian billionaire sanctioned by the U.S. in late 2024: Bidzina Ivanishvili.

When the developers struck a 2023 deal to buy the land from a foundation controlled by Ivanishvili's family, they agreed to pay the foundation up to $85 million at a later date, Georgian corporate records show. The developers paid in installments over time, and the deal was fully completed in July, a spokeswoman for the project said.

Ivanishvili is widely viewed by analysts as being the ultimate decision maker in the country. He made a fortune in Russia before he served as Georgia's prime minister between 2012 and 2013. Since leaving office, he has served as the honorary chairman of Georgian Dream, the party he founded.

Ivanishvili, whose mansion overlooks Tbilisi, has also been blamed for a sometimes violent crackdown on the political opposition. Georgian Dream was accused of election fraud in a 2024 vote that has sparked nearly two years of regular street protests. Georgian Dream has said the election victory was legitimate.

The U.S. House of Representatives last year moved to further punish Georgia's political leaders, passing a bill with bipartisan support that directed the U.S. government to consider sanctions on current and former members of the Georgian parliament, among other political leaders.
"The Georgian Dream insults President Trump every day with its anti-American propaganda," U.S. Rep. Joe Wilson, a Republican congressman from South Carolina who backed the bill, said in a statement.
Representatives of Ivanishvili and Georgian Dream didn't respond to requests for comment.

The tower marks the second attempt by developers to build a Trump skyscraper in the country. Fifteen years ago, developers in the Black Sea resort city of Batumi paid the Trump Organization a roughly $1 million upfront fee to brand their tower Trump. The branding deal later fell apart.

The latest rendition came about after New York developer Alex Sapir visited Georgia last year and met with local developers, a person familiar with the development said. Sapir's family, originally from Georgia, built the Trump SoHo in New York and the real estate scion introduced the group to the Trump Organization.

Months of back and forth followed, and in May a group of Georgian investors-including Samson Pkhakadze, president of the conglomerate Wissol Group, and Ilia Tsulaia, a former member of parliament aligned with Georgian Dream-flew to South Florida to sign an agreement with Eric Trump at Mar-a-Lago.
Tsulaia said in a statement announcing the deal in May that the tower would create a "landmark that will transform the skyline and elevate Georgia's presence on the global stage."

Georgian analysts see the deal as a way of the business community making something of a peace offering to the Trump administration, signaling that they are still eager to keep an open relationship with the U.S. at a time that diplomatic channels have been strained.

"This project is mainly about having some kind of connection with the Trump administration," said Giorgi Khishtovani, an economist and professor at Ilia State University in Tbilisi. "Its purpose may also be for PR reasons too."

While the government has indeed moved closer to Russia and shelved plans to join the European Union, Tbilisi is wary of becoming too reliant on Moscow while a fifth of its territory remains under Russian occupation since a 2008 invasion.
Tsulaia himself was part of a delegation last year that went to Washington to push the virtues of better Georgian-U.S. ties with lawmakers and administration officials.

During that visit, the delegation made clear they were interested in finding ways to smooth a better relationship with the new administration in Washington and get sanctions relief, said a former U.S. official involved in the talks. "There's different flavors for each country," the former official said. "They want a positive embrace."
